title: Catching the repricing wave: insights from daily online supermarket prices
author: European Central Bank
text:
THE ECB BLOGCatching the repricing wave: insights from daily online supermarket prices2 November 2026By Chiara Osbat, Christian Höynck, Umberto Maglione and Elisabeth WielandHas the latest energy shock triggered a new wave of food price increases? To find out, we’ve used innovative AI tools to track changes in price setting by supermarkets. So far, the rise in the repricing momentum has been weaker than in 2022, following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.When an energy price shock hits the economy, food prices are among the first to rise. That has immediate consequences for consumers. Food accounts for around 20% of expenditure in the euro area consumption basket used to calculate the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices (HICP). And this share is even larger for low-income households.[1] Charalambakis, E., Fagandini, B., Henkel, L. and Osbat, C. (2022), “The impact of the recent rise in inflation on low-income households”, Economic Bulletin, Box 4, Issue 7, ECB; and Bobasu, A., Di Nino, V. and Osbat, C. (2023), “The impact of the recent inflation surge across households”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 3, ECB. As such, changing food prices play a key role in influencing households’ perceptions and expectations surrounding inflation.[2] See Arce, O., Koester, G. and Nickel, C. (2023), “One year since Russia’s invasion of Ukraine – the effects on euro area inflation”, ECB Blog, 24 February; Bobeica, E., Koester, G. and Nickel, C. (2025), “When groceries bite: the role of food prices for inflation in the euro area”, ECB Blog, 25 September; Bates, C., Kuik, F., Wieland, E. and Zekaite, Z. (2025), “Inside the food basket: what is behind recent food inflation?”, Economic Bulletin, Box 7, Issue 8, ECB; and Lane, P.R. (2026), “Analytical perspectives on energy supply shocks”, dinner remarks at the Centre for European Reform, London, 13 May. Meanwhile, from a monetary policy perspective, it is crucial to understand the pattern of a repricing wave. Policymakers need to grasp how quickly firms adjust prices, how widespread those adjustments are and whether they might generate persistent inflationary pressures. But how can we capture repricing dynamics affecting consumers in real time when large shocks happen? The ECB has created a tool, the Daily Price Dataset (DPD), to follow supermarket price developments as they unfold. Since 2022 the DPD has provided information about how firms reset prices and on the likelihood that inflation arising from the shock will be strong, broad-based and persistent.[3] See Osbat, C. (2022), “What micro price data teach us about the inflation process: web-scraping in PRISMA”, SUERF Policy Brief No 470, November; Strasser, G., Wieland, E., Macias, P., Blazejowska, A., Szafranek, K. and Wittekopf, D. (2023), “E-commerce and price setting: evidence from Europe”, SUERF Policy Brief, No 698, October; Dedola, L., Henkel, L., Höynck, C., Osbat, C. and Santoro, S. (2024), “What does new micro price evidence tell us about inflation dynamics and monetary policy transmission?”, Economic Bulletin, Issue 3, ECB; Gautier, E., Conflitti, C., Enderle, D., Fadejeva, L., Grimaud, A., Gutiérrez, E., Jouvanceau, V., Menz, J.O., Paulus, A., Petroulas, P., Roldan-Blanco, P. and Wieland, W. (2026), “Consumer price stickiness in the euro area during an inflation surge”, Working Paper Series, No 3181, ECB, Frankfurt am Main, February; and Karadi, P., Amann, J., Sánchez Bachiller, J., Seiler, P. and Wursten, J. (2023), “Price setting on the two sides of the Atlantic – evidence from supermarket scanner data”, Journal of Monetary Economics, Vol. 140, Supplement, pp. S1-S17. Our tool indicates that the ongoing resetting of food prices triggered by the energy shock arising from the war in the Middle East is weaker than that in 2022 following the Russian invasion of Ukraine. The data show that initially food repricing increased fairly broadly but then stabilised. This contrasts with what happened during the 2022 energy shock, when the repricing wave continued to rise.How do firms react to a cost shock?Following a cost shock, firms decide whether they will adjust their prices and by how much. They make decisions based on factors such as the size of the shock, competitors’ prices and the costs of changing prices (so-called “menu costs”). If shocks are small, firms will not deviate from their regular repricing plans, but if they are large, they will want to adjust prices earlier than planned (so-called “state-dependent pricing”). In this case, we will observe an increase in the frequency of price increases, leading to non-linear effects on the inflation response that are relevant for monetary policy. Two aspects are especially informative. The first is how often firms raise and lower prices, known as the extensive margin. The second is the size of those price changes, known as the intensive margin. Together, these reveal the answer to the following question: is observed inflation the outcome of a few, very large price increases or of a broad-based repricing wave across products and retailers?To address this question, ECB staff in the PRISMA research network developed the DPD, working with the BIS Innovation Hub and the Deutsche Bundesbank under Project Spectrum.[4] See ECB (2026), “Price-setting Microdata Analysis Network (PRISMA)” and BIS (2026), “Project Spectrum. Using generative AI to enhance inflation nowcasting”. The dataset uses daily online supermarket prices and an AI-based classifier that maps retailers’ product descriptions onto consumption categories underlying the HICP basket.It measures the resulting repricing frequencies monthly to remove short-lived fluctuations, including temporary sales. However, because the tool collects underlying observations every day, it can update the estimate for the current month continuously throughout the month.[5] Price-change frequencies and sizes exclude temporary sales. Country and category aggregates are calculated using HICP expenditure weights. 2026 versus 2022: what does the DPD tell us?The frequency of food price increases rose in March 2026, shortly after the energy shock hit (Chart 1, panel a). However, this increase was much smaller than during the inflation surge of 2022. In contrast, the gap between the frequency of price increases and decreases is small. The average size of price increases changed relatively little, similar to the 2022 episode (Chart 1, panel b). Chart 1Frequency and size of food price changes over timea) frequency of food price changes b) average size of non-zero price changesSources: Eurostat, ECB Daily Price Dataset (DPD) and BIS Project Spectrum.Notes: The dotted lines show the month-on-month frequency of price changes; the solid lines show the corresponding three-month moving averages. Frequencies and sizes exclude price changes due to temporary sales. Country and category aggregates are calculated using HICP expenditure weights. The latest observations are for September 2026.Chart 2 provides a broader view by grouping food categories according to the frequency of price increases. The yellow areas show the share in the food basket of categories in which 10% or more of individual product prices increased in the month.During the 2022 inflation surge, these shares expanded and remained large for several months. This indicated a broad and persistent shift towards more frequent price adjustments. Such behaviour is consistent with state-dependent price-setting by firms in the euro area during the 2021-24 inflation cycle.[6] This is documented by Gautier, E., Conflitti, C., Enderle, D., Fadejeva, L., Grimaud, A., Gutiérrez, E., Jouvanceau, V., Menz, J.-O., Paulus, A., Petroulas, P., Roldan-Blanco, P. and Wieland, E. (2026), “Consumer price stickiness in the euro area during an inflation surge”, Working Paper Series, No 3181, ECB, Frankfurt am Main, February. Chart 2Share of individual items in the HICP food basket grouped by frequency of price increases(percentages)Sources: Eurostat, ECB Daily Price Dataset (DPD) and BIS Project Spectrum.Notes: The month-on-month frequency of price increases excludes price changes due to temporary sales. Country and category aggregates are calculated using HICP expenditure weights. The latest observations are for September 2026.Chart 3, which shows the distribution of repricing frequencies across individual food categories, indicates that while there was an initial rise in March 2026, the frequency of price increases did not rise and widen sequentially in 2026 as it did in 2022.The range of price changes is overall more compressed in 2026 compared with 2022, and the maximum frequency of price changes is also far lower in most months of 2026.Chart 3Distribution of the frequency of price increases across food categories in 2022 and 2026(month-on-month frequency of price increases, percentages)Sources: Eurostat, ECB Daily Price Dataset (DPD), and BIS Project Spectrum.Notes: Each box summarises the distribution across food categories of the month-on-month frequency of price increases (excluding price changes due to temporary sales). The boxes represent the inter-quartile range across consumption categories, and the whiskers show the minimum and maximum of the range. Country and category aggregates are calculated using HICP expenditure weights. The latest observations are for September 2026.ConclusionFor monetary policy, after an energy shock we need to ask whether higher costs are triggering a broad and persistent repricing response and non-linear inflation dynamics. To answer that question, it is essential to establish not only that the inflation rate has increased, but also through which margins. This is because inflation can rise owing to more frequent repricing, larger individual price changes, broad-based increases or large surges in very specific products. The ECB’s DPD provides an early indication of which of these margins are driving inflation.Following the 2026 energy shock, we find little evidence so far of a persistent change in how often retailers reprice food items, in contrast to 2022. This contrast between 2022 and 2026 is consistent with the broader finding that the effects of an energy shock depend on the composition of the shock itself as well as on the economic conditions prevailing when it occurs.[7] See Arce, O., Battistini, N., Bouabdallah, O., Lis, E. and Mohr, M. (2026), “A tale of two energy crises – initial conditions matter”, ECB Blog, 3 June.
